plain_title: When a young person keeps breaking rules and hurting others
one_liner: A repeated pattern in a child or teen of aggression, destruction, lying, theft, or serious rule-breaking over a year.
in_simple_words: Conduct disorder is diagnosed in children and teens who keep breaking important rules for a year or more. That can mean fighting, cruelty, damaging property, lying, stealing, running away, or skipping school. It often grows out of ODD, ADHD, trauma, or a chaotic home. It is far more common among young people who have been abused or in care. Early, family-based help works. Most young people do not go on to adult problems.
what_it_can_feel_like: He wasn't born like this. By the time anyone offered help he'd been excluded from three schools.
I was angry at everyone, so I made sure everyone was scared of me. I was 13 and I'd never felt safe a day in my life.
Multisystemic therapy was the first thing that treated us as a family instead of treating my son as a criminal.
common_signs: Aggression toward people or animals: bullying, fighting, cruelty, or using weapons
Destroying property or setting fires deliberately
Serious rule-breaking: staying out, running away, skipping school, before age 13
Pattern over at least a year causing real harm or trouble

myths_vs_facts.myth: Conduct disorder means a child is a lost cause.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Most young people with conduct disorder do not go on to adult antisocial behaviour, and the earlier the help, the better the outcome.

myths_vs_facts.myth: These kids need tougher punishment or boot camp.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Research shows harsh, scare-based programmes don't work and can make things worse. Family and skills-based therapies do work.
Genetics, early trauma, learning difficulties, poverty, neighbourhood, and peers all contribute. Blaming parents drives families away from the help that works.

how_common.plain: Around 4 in 100 children and teens have conduct disorder, by most estimates, more boys than girls. Rates are much higher among young people who've experienced abuse or care.
how_common.figure: About 4% median prevalence, range 2%–10% (DSM-5-TR text); nearly 40% of looked-after or abused children in a 2004 UK survey (NICE CG158 context)

what_helps.plain_summary: NICE and other guidelines recommend parent training programmes for younger children, and for teens, family-based treatments such as multisystemic therapy or functional family therapy, which work with the whole family, school, and community. Child-focused skills therapy helps with problem solving and emotions. Co-occurring ADHD, depression, trauma, and learning difficulties are treated. Medication isn't a treatment for conduct disorder itself, and if used for aggression it's prescribed and monitored by a specialist.
evidence_based_options: Parent training programmes for children aged roughly 3 to 11
Multisystemic therapy or functional family therapy for adolescents
Child-focused problem-solving and emotion skills programmes
Treatment of ADHD, trauma, depression, or learning difficulties
self_help_that_supports_care: Keeping one trusted adult relationship steady, whatever happens
Structure: school attendance, sport, something the young person is good at
Parents getting their own support and respite
Avoiding punishment that cuts the young person off from everyone

when_to_reach_out: If a child or teen is repeatedly aggressive, destructive, or in trouble with school or the law, ask a doctor, school, or children's mental health service for an assessment, and ask specifically about family-based treatments. If anyone is in immediate danger, call emergency services.
is_not: A single serious incident, teenage rule-bending, behaviour that's a direct response to abuse or danger, or difficulties explained by autism, ADHD, or a learning disability aren't conduct disorder on their own.
hope_note: Many young people once labelled 'the problem kid' go on to steady work, families, and lives their younger selves couldn't picture.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.
Behaviour labels carry stigma for children and families; wording reviewed for blame.

in_young_people: This is a diagnosis of childhood and adolescence. Childhood onset (before 10) tends to be more persistent than adolescent onset; both respond to treatment.

sub_sections.title: 'With limited prosocial emotions' specifier
sub_sections.text: Added when a young person shows persistent lack of remorse, empathy, or concern about performance. It points to a need for more intensive, specialised support, not a verdict about character.
